source.title: Broken Ergodicity and the Violation of the Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem Lead to Generalization Beyond Overfitting in Machine Learning

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplemental material are present. There are minor typesetting/OCR glitches in equations, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes generalization and training error around an interpolation threshold using dynamical mean-field theory and simulations of single-layer linear regression, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own capacity-dependent and time-dependent error results, regularization results, and response/FDT results. Results cited from other work are not recorded. Numerical points visible only in figures are not transcribed where the text gives no exact values.
record.test_reason: The paper derives, with dynamical mean-field theory checked against SGD simulations, the test error of teacher–student linear regression as a function of the capacity ratio α = d/N. It finds a divergent peak at the interpolation threshold α = 1 and a descent beyond it. It also reports how label-noise variance D and ℓ2 strength λ shape that peak. This is a different method aimed at the same question, in a non-deep model class.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors interpret double descent in unregularized SGD-trained linear regression as a dynamical phase transition at α = 1, with critical exponents σ = 1 and ϕ = 2. Below the threshold, error is set by a diverging susceptibility. Above it, broken ergodicity and persistent memory of initialization explain 'benign overfitting'. They treat ℓ2 regularization as a finite-size field that rounds and shifts the peak. Universality across architectures is conjectured, not shown.
record.recipe_differences: Uses dynamical mean-field theory and teacher–student single-layer linear regression, with analytical calculations and simulations; it does not reproduce the original deep-network experiments or their method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported peak is changed by regularization strength: finite λ rounds the divergence and shifts the peak slightly leftward. Stochasticity γ rescales time in the unregularized case; under regularization, the authors report that stochasticity also affects final generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Above α = 1 the long-time response plateaus at (α−1)/α and the fluctuation–dissipation theorem fails; below α = 1 it holds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In unregularized linear regression, the interpolation threshold coincides with a dynamical transition to broken ergodicity, with persistent memory of initialization.

fits_no_version.finding: With λ = 0, SGD stochasticity γ only rescales time and leaves asymptotic test error unchanged. With λ > 0, the authors say stochasticity also changes final generalization (no numbers given).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SGD noise affects the height of the double-descent curve only when explicit regularization is present.

record.problems: The tested model is a single-layer linear teacher–student regression model, and the authors state that it lacks the first descent of the classical bias–variance tradeoff. Most capacity and time plots do not have exact point values in the text; simulations are reported with averages over ten runs in several figures, while Fig. 4 uses 50 runs and bootstrap error bars.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the row limit. Individual numerical points available only in plots are not transcribed; relevant explicit formulas and described outcomes are recorded instead.

untested.parts: No deep networks. Only a single-layer linear teacher–student model is studied.
The full shape of test error over training time (fall-rise-fall) is not resolved. Only long-time asymptotics and saturation are given.
No sample-count sweep is reported. The theory depends only on α = d/N, which implies more data can raise error for α > 1 near 1, but the paper does not present or test this.
Only one model class (linear regression) is studied. There is no survey across model classes.
Susceptibility is linked to error along α only. No single complexity measure is tested as predicting peaks across size, epochs and samples.
Multiple peaks are not studied. Removal of the peak under optimally tuned regularization is not tested (only weak λ in the peak-height analysis).
No re-expression of the curve against an effective parameter count.

missing.what: Dependence of peak height on label-noise variance D (divergent terms proportional to D; time curves for D = 1, 0.5, 0.1)
missing.locator: Main text Eqs. 6–7; Supplemental Eqs. S164–S166; Fig. S1

missing.what: Static and dynamic scaling collapse of steady-state test error under λ ∈ [0.01, 1], with deviations at larger λ
Non-monotone overparameterized branch: the (α−1)C(0,0)/α term grows with α, so large-α error approaches C(0,0)+D
missing.locator: Main text Eq. 7; Fig. 1a (α up to 5)

record.verdict_notes: V1 links were removed throughout: the system is a linear model, not a deep network, so model-wise results are credited to V4. The reader's V2 'challenges' was dropped: the √t growth at α = 1 is an asymptote, and the early-time shape is not reported. Training-error rows R3–R5 only confirm the interpolation point. The large-α turn-up and the comparison with small-α error come from our arithmetic on Eq. 7 with the Fig. 1 parameters; researchers should verify this. Because error depends only on α = d/N, the theory implicitly predicts sample-wise non-monotonicity (V3), but the paper never reports a sample sweep.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests capacity-dependent error in a single-layer linear network, not deep networks or other architectures; the underparameterized side lacks the classical first descent.
It reports time evolution and critical growth or saturation, but does not establish a fall-rise-fall curve over epochs.
No sweep of training sample count near the interpolation threshold is reported.
It tests a linear-regression model class and the post-interpolation descent, but not a classical initial descent in this setting or a broad survey across model classes.
The study relates susceptibility to generalization error, but does not test one effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.

Regularization effects on the capacity-dependent peak are reported. The study does not test whether label noise drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The study does not re-express the curve using an appropriate effective parameter count or show that this converts it to an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: single-layer linear neural network
rows.operation_detail: Analytically evaluated the asymptotic generalization error as capacity ratio α varies, with λ = 0.
rows.note: As α increases toward 1 from below, this expression rises, rather than showing an initial descent. The authors state that this well-specified regime lacks the first descent of the classical bias–variance tradeoff.
rows.check: The subject is a single-layer linear model, not a deep network, so the link to V1 is removed. 'Reversed' is wrong. Error rising as α→1⁻ (D/(1−α)) is the expected approach to the peak. What is missing is the classical first descent: the authors say the well-specified model lacks it.

rows.operation_detail: Analytically evaluated the asymptotic generalization error as capacity ratio α varies, with λ = 0.
rows.locator: Main text, Eq. (7); Supplemental Material, Eqs. (S165)–(S166); Fig. 1(a)
rows.note: The authors state that error decreases from a divergence near α = 1 as capacity increases into the overparameterized regime. C(0,0) depends on initialization and the teacher norm.
rows.check: V1 link removed because the system is not a deep network. Eq. 7 falls from the divergence just above α = 1, but its term (α−1)C(0,0)/α grows with α. With Fig. 1 settings (D = 1, C(0,0) = 2, by our calculation) error bottoms near 2.83 at α≈3.4. It then rises toward C(0,0)+D = 3. It never drops below the small-α value D = 1. This is our calculation from the study's own formula; the paper does not state it.

relationships.condition: Unregularized linear regression, α just above the interpolation threshold
relationships.reason: R2: asymptotic test error falls from its divergence at α = 1 as capacity grows into the overparameterized regime (Eq. 7, Fig. 1a).
relationships.display_finding: Asymptotic test error decreased from its divergence at α = 1 as capacity increased into the overparameterized regime.

relationships.reason: R1: no classical first descent; error only rises toward α = 1, so the curve does not subsume a U-shape here.
relationships.display_finding: Error rose toward α = 1 without a classical first descent.

relationships.condition: Large α with nonzero random initialization (Fig. 1 settings)
relationships.reason: R2: by our calculation from Eq. 7, error has a minimum near α≈3.4 (≈2.83), then rises toward C(0,0)+D = 3. It never falls below the small-α error D = 1.
relationships.display_finding: Calculations from Equation 7 gave a minimum near α ≈ 3.4 with error ≈ 2.83, followed by an increase toward 3; error never fell below the small-α value of 1.

relationships.condition: Label-noise dependence of the peak, λ = 0
relationships.reason: Based on the text (no row): the divergent terms in Eqs. 6–7 are D/(1−α) and Dα/(α−1), so the peak scales with label-noise variance. With D = 0 the peak vanishes.
relationships.display_finding: The divergent terms D/(1−α) and Dα/(α−1) scaled with label-noise variance, and the peak vanished at D=0.

relationships.reason: R8: regularization rounds the divergence into a finite peak with height ∝ λ^−1/2. This is consistent with regularization suppressing the peak; removal at optimal λ was not tested.
relationships.display_finding: Weak regularization rounded the divergence into a finite peak whose height scaled as λ^-1/2.
